Regarding the distractors, a linear or fissured fracture (Option B) appears as a simple crack or radiolucent line without any displacement of the bone. A hinge fracture (Option C) is a base-of-skull fracture that runs transversely from one side to the other, usually not visible in this vault view. A gutter fracture (Option D) is a specific type of groove in the bone typically caused by an oblique gunshot wound. Because the image clearly shows the "stepping" of the bone inward, it is categorized as a depressed fracture

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A TB patient with HIV begins ART and experiences deterioration in health after 2 months. What is the likely cause?
options: Development of drug resistance to TB drugs
Drug-drug interactions between TB and ART medications
Development of drug resistance to ART
questions.explanation: The clinical deterioration seen roughly two months after initiating Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) in an HIV-TB co-infected patient is most likely due to Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). This condition arises from immunological changes where the recovering immune system mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against the pre-existing Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Symptoms typically include worsening fever and enlarging lymph nodes. Regarding the distractors, drug resistance (Options A and D) generally develops over a longer period and presents with a failure to clear the viral or bacterial load rather than an acute inflammatory flare. While drug-drug interactions (Option B) between rifampicin and certain ART drugs like protease inhibitors are common, they typically lead to therapeutic failure rather than the paradoxical clinical worsening characteristic of IRIS. Management involves continuing both treatments while managing inflammation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man develops headache, nausea, and breathlessness while trekking at high altitude. To relieve his symptoms, the physician prescribes a medication. This drug primarily acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from acute mountain sickness (AMS) due to high-altitude hypoxia. The standard pharmacological intervention is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that primarily acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron. By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the PCT, the drug prevents bicarbonate reabsorption, leading to mild metabolic acidosis. This acidosis stimulates the central respiratory centers, prompting compensatory hyperventilation which increases blood oxygenation and alleviates AMS symptoms. Regarding the distractors, loop diuretics (Option B), thiazides (Option C), and potassium-sparing diuretics (Option D) act on different segments of the nephron and do not address the physiological causes of altitude sickness. Therefore, the PCT is the specific site where acetazolamide exerts its therapeutic effect for mountain climbers

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with symmetrical flaccid weakness of the lower limbs along with absence of spinal cord reflexes. This clinical presentation is suggestive of which condition?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of symmetric lower limb flaccidity and areflexia (no cord reflex) are characteristic of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy that causes demyelination of peripheral nerves. It typically presents as a "ground-to-brain" ascending paralysis, beginning with weakness in the legs. Multiple sclerosis (Option B) is a central nervous system disorder that usually presents with upper motor neuron signs like spasticity and hyperreflexia. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) involves both upper and lower motor neuron signs but typically presents with asymmetric onset and fasciculations. Spinal cord injury (Option D) usually presents with a clear sensory and motor level and, after the initial shock phase, leads to spasticity rather than persistent flaccidity. Thus, the rapid onset of symmetric flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes is a clinical hallmark of the peripheral nerve involvement seen in GBS

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted with fever and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals low glucose levels, elevated protein, and a predominance of neutrophils. What is the most appropriate treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, combined with CSF findings of decreased glucose, elevated protein, and neutrophilic pleocytosis, is diagnostic of bacterial meningitis. Ceftriaxone is the first-line, broad-spectrum antibiotic recommended for empirical treatment in adults. It effectively covers the most common pathogens, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Regarding the distractors, Ampicillin (Option A) is specifically added for Listeria monocytogenes in neonates or elderly patients but is not the primary choice for standard adult cases. Penicillin (Option C) is no longer used alone due to rising resistance. Vancomycin (Option D) is often used with Ceftriaxone to cover penicillin-resistant strains but is insufficient as monotherapy. Therefore, Ceftriaxone is the most appropriate first-line agent based on the provided clinical and laboratory profile

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman attends the clinic for a routine follow-up. She has well-controlled mild hypertension and denies symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness, or chest pain. An ECG recording is provided. Based on the ECG findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The ECG characteristically shows a prolonged PR interval exceeding 0.20 seconds (5 small squares). Crucially, every P wave is followed by a QRS complex, meaning there are no dropped beats. This consistent delay without conduction failure is diagnostic of First-Degree AV Block. Regarding the distractors, Second-Degree AV Block (Option A) would show intermittent dropped beats (e.g., Mobitz I or II). Third-Degree AV Block (Option C) would show complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes. Bundle Branch Block (Option D) is characterized by a widened QRS complex ( s), which is not present here. Since the patient is asymptomatic and the conduction is stable, First-Degree AV Block is the most likely finding, typically requiring only routine observation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with fluctuating muscle weakness predominantly involving speech and swallowing. Repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrates a decremental response. Serological testing is negative for acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies. Which other antibody is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—fluctuating weakness in speech and swallowing (bulbar symptoms) and a decremental response on nerve stimulation—are typical of Myasthenia Gravis. In patients who are seronegative for AChR antibodies, the Anti-MuSK (Muscle-Specific Kinase) antibody is the most likely culprit. MuSK is essential for clustering AChRs at the neuromuscular junction; its inhibition disrupts signal transmission. Regarding the distractors, Anti-dsDNA (Option A) is a marker for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-TPO (Option C) is associated with autoimmune thyroiditis. Anti-Ro (Option D) is found in Sjogren's syndrome. Because MuSK-positive patients often present with severe bulbar involvement and are negative for the standard AChR test, this antibody specifically matches the patient's clinical and laboratory profile

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which electrolyte abnormality will lead to cardiac arrhythmia in patients with severe vomiting?
questions.explanation: Severe vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), resulting in metabolic alkalosis. This alkalosis causes an intracellular shift of potassium, which, combined with increased renal potassium excretion to compensate for the bicarbonate load, leads to profound hypokalemia. Low serum potassium disrupts the cardiac membrane potential and repolarization, making it a major risk factor for life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Typical ECG changes in hypokalemia include flattened T waves, prominent U waves, and a prolonged QT interval, which can lead to Torsades de Pointes. Hyponatremia (Option B) can occur due to volume loss but is less likely to cause direct arrhythmias. Hyperkalemia (Option C) typically results from renal failure or acidosis, not vomiting. Hypocalcemia (Option D) causes QT prolongation and tetany but is not the primary drive for arrhythmias in the setting of gastric acid loss. Treatment focuses on replacing potassium and correcting the underlying fluid deficit

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child is brought to the emergency department with vomiting and loose stools, along with a history of laxative use. On examination, the child is found to have an arrhythmia. What underlying abnormality is most likely present?
questions.explanation: The combination of vomiting, loose stools, chronic laxative use, and cardiac arrhythmia in a child strongly suggests hypokalemia. Hypokalemia is defined as a serum potassium level below 3.5 mEq/L and is a very common result of significant gastrointestinal fluid losses. Low potassium levels disrupt the resting membrane potential of cardiac myocytes, leading to delayed repolarization and life-threatening arrhythmias in severe cases. Hyponatremia (Option A) can occur with GI losses but is not characteristically associated with direct cardiac arrhythmias. Hypocalcemia (Option B) classically presents with neuromuscular irritability (tetany) and a prolonged QT interval but is not the primary driver of arrhythmias in this context. Hyperkalemia (Option D) also causes arrhythmias, but it results from renal failure or acidosis rather than the potassium depletion seen with vomiting and laxatives. Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L) requires urgent intravenous potassium chloride replacement with careful monitoring

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to the American Heart Association (AHA), what is the 6th link added to the chain of survival?
questions.explanation: The American Heart Association (AHA) expanded the Chain of Survival concept by adding a sixth link: recovery and rehabilitation. This addition reflects the growing recognition that survival extends far beyond the immediate resuscitation period. The complete AHA Chain of Survival now includes early recognition and activation of emergency response, high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced life support, post-cardiac arrest care, and finally, recovery and rehabilitation. Rapid defibrillation (Option A) is already included as the critical third link. High-quality CPR (Option C) constitutes the second link, emphasizing proper depth and rate. Advanced airway management (Option D) is part of the fourth link (advanced life support) but should never interfere with or delay chest compressions and defibrillation. Therefore, the newly introduced sixth link acknowledges the long-term support needed for survivors

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old man is brought to the hospital with auditory hallucinations and difficulty recognizing his family members. He has a history of chronic alcohol use and reports that his last alcohol consumption was 48 hours ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s auditory hallucinations and severe confusion occurring 48 hours after his last drink strongly suggest Delirium Tremens (DTs). DTs is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically peaking between 48 and 96 hours. It is characterized by altered mental status, disorientation, and autonomic hyperactivity. Alcoholic hallucinosis (Option B) involves hallucinations with an intact orientation and usually occurs earlier, within 12–24 hours. Alcohol-induced psychosis (Option C) refers to persistent psychotic symptoms due to chronic use rather than acute withdrawal instability. Schizophrenia (Option D) is a chronic disorder; the acute onset immediately following alcohol cessation makes a withdrawal syndrome far more probable. DTs is a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines and intensive care due to high mortality from cardiovascular collapse

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with hypertension is found to have laboratory abnormalities including hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Conn’s syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is the classic diagnosis for a hypertensive patient with hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Excess aldosterone secretion, usually from an adrenal adenoma, leads to increased sodium reabsorption (causing hypertension and hypernatremia) and increased renal excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. Addison’s disease (Option B) is the opposite; it presents with hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Diabetes Insipidus (Option C) causes hypernatremia due to free water loss but is not associated with hypertension, hypokalemia, or metabolic alkalosis. Cushing’s disease (Option D) primarily involves excess cortisol; while it can cause hypertension, it does not typically present with this specific triad of electrolyte and acid-base disturbances unless there is very severe ectopic ACTH production. Therefore, primary aldosterone overproduction is the most probable physiological explanation for these laboratory findings

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of recurrent vomiting undergoes arterial blood gas analysis, which shows a pH of 7.5, PaCO₂ of 48 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ of 30 mm Hg. Based on these findings, what is the most likely acid–base disorder?
questions.explanation: The blood gas findings show an elevated pH (7.5), confirming alkalosis. The primary cause is an elevated bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) of 30 mEq/L, which results from the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) during vomiting. The body responds through respiratory compensation—hypoventilation to retain —which explains the elevated of 48 mm Hg. Metabolic acidosis (Option B) would feature a low pH and low . Respiratory acidosis (Option C) is characterized by a low pH and high . Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) involves a high pH with a low due to hyperventilation. Thus, the clinical context of vomiting combined with the metabolic laboratory values clearly points to metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation as the most likely acid-base disturbance in this patient

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which clinical or investigative factor is most helpful in differentiating acute kidney injury (AKI) from chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
questions.explanation: Albumin levels are a highly useful differentiating factor, as persistent hypoalbuminemia and significant albuminuria (30 mg/24 hours) are defining characteristics of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). In contrast, albumin levels in Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) often remain relatively normal unless there is pre-existing damage. Creatinine (Option A) and BUN (Option D) are elevated in both conditions, making them unreliable for differentiation based on a single measurement. While urinary output (Option C) can decrease in both, oliguria is more sudden and common in AKI, but can also occur in end-stage CKD. CKD is defined by structural or functional abnormalities persisting for more than 3 months, whereas AKI is an abrupt rise in creatinine over 48 hours. Therefore, chronic protein loss makes low albumin a hallmark of CKD

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the context of mitral stenosis, which clinical feature is typically observed?
questions.explanation: A loud, snapping first heart sound (S1) is a hallmark of mitral stenosis. This occurs because the mitral leaflets are thickened but still mobile, and the high pressure gradient in the left atrium causes them to slam shut forcefully at the start of systole. An absent S1 (Option B) is more characteristic of severe mitral regurgitation where the leaflets fail to coapt. An S3 gallop (Option C) is associated with volume overload and heart failure, which is not typical for the restricted filling of mitral stenosis. Muffled heart sounds (Option D) suggest pericardial effusion or severe obesity. Other classic findings of mitral stenosis include an opening snap and a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with a Graham-Steel murmur?
questions.explanation: The Graham-Steel murmur is a high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation in the setting of severe pulmonary hypertension. It is heard best at the left upper sternal border. Ventricular septal defect (Option A) classically causes a harsh holosystolic murmur. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (Option B) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that increases with the Valsalva maneuver. Aortic regurgitation (Option D) also causes a diastolic decrescendo murmur, but it is heard at the right upper or left mid-sternal border and may be associated with an "Austin Flint" murmur at the apex. Therefore, the Graham-Steel murmur specifically indicates pulmonary valve incompetence resulting from dilation of the pulmonary artery due to high pressure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a recent history of throat infection presents with a characteristic water hammer pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A "water hammer" (collapsing) pulse, also known as Corrigan's pulse, is pathognomonic for aortic regurgitation. The history of a throat infection points to a prior streptococcal infection triggering rheumatic fever, which is a major cause of valvular damage, particularly affecting the aortic valve. Infective endocarditis (Option B) can cause aortic regurgitation but usually presents with acute fever and embolic signs like splinter hemorrhages. Mitral stenosis (Option C) classically presents with a small, low-volume pulse rather than a collapsing one. Aortic stenosis (Option D) features a "pulsus parvus et tardus," which is slow-rising and low-amplitude. The water hammer pulse results from the rapid ejection of a large stroke volume into the aorta followed by immediate backflow into the left ventricle during diastole

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The CSF findings in bacterial meningitis would include which of the following?
options: Elevated WBC count with normal glucose
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis is characterized by distinct cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) abnormalities: elevated protein levels (>100 mg/dL) due to blood-brain barrier disruption and decreased glucose (<40% of blood glucose) because of utilization by bacteria and neutrophils. It also features a high white blood cell count, predominantly polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). Options B and D are incorrect because the glucose level is almost always low in bacterial infections. Option C is the opposite of the typical finding. In contrast, viral meningitis (Option D-like) usually has normal glucose and a lymphocyte predominance. Fungal or tubercular meningitis also has low glucose but typically features lymphocyte predominance rather than the high PMNs seen in bacterial causes. Therefore, the combination of high protein and low glucose is the classic biochemical hallmark of bacterial meningitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with Cryptococcal meningitis. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: The standard induction therapy for Cryptococcal meningitis is the combination of Flucytosine and Liposomal Amphotericin B (L.Amp) for 2 weeks. This combination is superior in rapidly clearing the fungal load from the CSF. Flucytosine (Option A) or L.Amp (Option C) alone are less effective and associated with higher mortality. Fluconazole (Option B) is used for the subsequent maintenance phase (typically 8–10 weeks) after the initial induction is complete, but it is not the first-line induction treatment. Cryptococcal meningitis is a major opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients and is diagnosed by CSF India ink staining or antigen tests. Managing increased intracranial pressure via frequent lumbar punctures is also a critical adjunctive management step alongside this combination antifungal regimen

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old female visited the clinician with a solitary thyroid nodule and was advised for thyroid function tests where TSH level is 27.3 mU/L, T3 is 1.24 ng/ml, and T4 is 4.87 microgram/ml. Which of the following manifestations is true regarding the condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s laboratory results show a significantly elevated TSH (27.3 mU/L) with normal to low-normal T3 and T4 levels, which is characteristic of primary hypothyroidism. Weight gain is a classic manifestation of hypothyroidism due to a decreased basal metabolic rate. Other typical symptoms include cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, and dry skin. In contrast, heat intolerance (Option A), tachycardia (Option B), and diarrhea (Option C) are hallmark symptoms of hyperthyroidism, where metabolic processes are accelerated. The most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in developed regions is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, while iodine deficiency remains a major cause globally. Given the high TSH, the body is attempting to stimulate a failing thyroid gland. Weight gain, puffiness, and lethargy are the most consistent clinical findings in this metabolic state

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with unilateral throbbing headache accompanied by photophobia, nausea, and vomiting, with symptomatic relief following the use of sumatriptan. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of unilateral, throbbing pain with sensory sensitivities like photophobia and gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea/vomiting is the classic presentation of a migraine headache. The patient’s specific response to sumatriptan further confirms this diagnosis. Sumatriptan is a selective 5-HT receptor agonist that acts as a vasoconstrictor to reverse the cerebral vasodilation that occurs during the headache phase. Tension headaches (Option B) are typically bilateral, feel like a "band" of pressure, and lack systemic symptoms. Cluster headaches (Option C) feature severe peri-orbital pain with autonomic signs like eye watering and nasal congestion. Sinus headaches (Option D) are associated with facial pressure and nasal discharge, not photophobia. Migraines can occur with or without an aura—neurologic disturbances like scintillating scotomas that often precede the pain

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a recent history of pneumonia develops a pleural effusion. On pleural fluid analysis, which finding is most characteristic of a parapneumonic effusion?
options: Pleural protein/plasma protein ratio less than 0.5
Pleural LDH less than 2/3rd of plasma LDH
Pleural LDH less than 0.6 of plasma LDH
questions.explanation: A pleural fluid pH of less than 7.2 is a critical indicator of a complicated parapneumonic effusion. This acidic state occurs because of increased metabolic activity by bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space, leading to lactic acid accumulation. According to Light’s Criteria, parapneumonic effusions are exudative, meaning they must have a pleural/serum protein ratio and a pleural/serum LDH ratio . Thus, Options A, B, and D are incorrect as they describe transudative characteristics. Complicated effusions often feature low glucose ( mg/dL) and high LDH levels ( U/L). Recognizing a low pH is essential because it serves as an absolute indication for chest tube drainage (thoracostomy) to prevent the development of a trapped lung or loculated empyema

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents with pain and swelling over the distal radius. Radiography reveals an expansile lytic lesion involving the metaphysis, and fine-needle aspiration yields a bloody aspirate containing hemosiderin-laden macrophages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign but aggressive expansile lytic lesion that most commonly involves the metaphysis of long bones. The diagnostic hallmark on FNA is a "bloody aspirate" containing hemosiderin-laden macrophages, reflecting the cystic, blood-filled nature of the lesion. Giant cell tumor (Option A) typically involves the epiphysis and lacks the significant hemosiderin deposits found on ABC aspirates. Osteosarcoma (Option C) is a malignant tumor presenting with mixed destruction and characteristic "sunburst" periosteal reactions rather than a purely cystic aspirate. Chondroblastoma (Option D) is a rare epiphyseal tumor that typically affects younger patients and shows chondroid matrix, not bloody cysts. MRI of an ABC often shows diagnostic "fluid-fluid levels" within multiple septations. Treatment involves thorough curettage and bone grafting

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with chronic stable angina reports worsening chest pain during routine activities despite being on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and atorvastatin. ECG shows ST-segment depression in leads V5–V6, and coronary angiography reveals an 80% stenosis of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent (DES)
Refer for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)
questions.explanation: The patient has significant stenosis (80%) of the LAD and persistent anginal symptoms despite being on optimal medical therapy. PCI with a drug-eluting stent (DES) is the most appropriate next step to restore blood flow and provide symptom relief. DES is preferred over bare-metal stents due to a lower risk of restenosis. Increasing beta-blockers (Option A) or adding ranolazine (Option B) would be insufficient given the severity of the anatomical obstruction and the persistence of symptoms. CABG (Option D) is typically reserved for more complex cases, such as three-vessel disease, significant left main disease, or patients with co-existing diabetes and multi-vessel involvement. For single-vessel LAD disease with preserved left ventricular function, PCI is highly effective and less invasive

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 72-year-old postmenopausal woman develops sudden severe chest pain and breathlessness following a stressful emotional event. She has no prior history of heart disease. On examination, she is mildly tachycardic with normal blood pressure. Echocardiography reveals systolic left ventricular apical ballooning, and cardiac enzymes are only minimally elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, or "broken heart syndrome," is a transient condition typically triggered by intense emotional or physical stress in post-menopausal women. It is characterized by the classic "ballooning" of the left ventricular apex during systole, resembling a Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo). Symptoms mimic an acute MI, including chest pain and minimal elevation of cardiac enzymes, yet coronary angiography typically shows no significant obstructive disease. Hypertensive heart disease (Option A) results from long-standing pressure and causes hypertrophy, not acute ballooning. Coronary artery disease (Option C) would feature significant plaque obstruction. Pulmonary embolism (Option D) causes acute pleuritic pain but not this specific LV wall motion abnormality. The condition is thought to be mediated by a massive catecholamine surge leading to microvascular dysfunction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with a known history of hypertension presents to the emergency department in acute distress. He is diaphoretic, tachycardic, and complains of severe chest pain. An ECG is provided. Based on his clinical condition and ECG findings, what is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation: The ECG shows classic "saw-tooth" F-waves at a rate of 150 bpm (2:1 conduction), which is pathognomonic for atrial flutter. The patient's presentation with acute distress, diaphoresis, and severe chest pain indicates that he is hemodynamically unstable. For an unstable patient with a supraventricular tachycardia like atrial flutter, synchronized cardioversion is the immediate treatment of choice to restore sinus rhythm. Amiodarone (Option A) and Digoxin (Option C) are used for rate or rhythm control in stable patients but are too slow for emergency stabilization. Radiofrequency ablation (Option B) is the definitive long-term treatment for preventing recurrence of atrial flutter but is not used in the acute setting. Immediate electrical intervention is required to prevent cardiovascular collapse

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old woman with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with a two-day history of worsening breathlessness, cough, and increased sputum production. She appears distressed, with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
options: Initiate high-flow oxygen therapy to maintain oxygen saturation above 95%
Start nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and ipratropium
Order a chest X-ray before any treatment is provided
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD, evidenced by increased breathlessness and sputum production. Nebulized bronchodilators are the first-line immediate therapy to relieve bronchospasm and improve air movement. Initiating high-flow oxygen to (Option A) is dangerous in COPD, as it can suppress the hypoxic respiratory drive, leading to life-threatening retention; oxygen should be controlled to a target of 88–92%. Glucocorticoids (Option C) are important but typically given orally and take hours to act, making them secondary to bronchodilators. While a chest X-ray (Option D) is necessary to rule out complications like pneumonia, it should not delay the initiation of life-saving bronchodilator therapy in a distressed patient. Immediate management focuses on airway relief and stabilized gas exchange

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends a routine follow-up visit. Investigations show normal serum creatinine and potassium levels, but microalbuminuria is present, and her HbA1c is 8%. Her blood pressure and pulse are within normal limits, and she is currently being treated with metformin. What should be the next step in her management?
options: Stop Metformin and start a different OHA
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits microalbuminuria, which is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy. Starting an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the critical next step, even if blood pressure is normal, because these drugs provide renoprotection by lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing the progression of albuminuria. Thiazide diuretics (Option A) may be used for edema but do not offer the same kidney-protective benefits. Insulin (Option B) is considered if HbA1c remains despite oral agents, which is not the case here. Metformin should only be stopped (Option C) if the eGFR falls below 30 ml/min, whereas this patient has normal creatinine. Early intervention with RAAS blockade significantly reduces the long-term risk of end-stage renal disease and major cardiovascular events in diabetics

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with a one-week history of fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia. Examination shows multiple purpura and petechiae over the shoulder, trunk, and legs, and there is a history of increased mosquito breeding with similar cases reported in the area. What is the most common neurological complication associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and petechial rashes linked to mosquito breeding are classic for Dengue fever. Dengue encephalopathy is the most frequently encountered neurological complication of the dengue virus. It is primarily linked to Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever and Dengue Shock Syndrome and is often metabolic in nature rather than a direct brain infection. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Option B), Stroke (Option C), and Encephalitis (Option D) are all recognized complications but occur less frequently than encephalopathy. Clinical features of dengue also include thrombocytopenia and plasma leakage leading to pleural effusion or ascites. Management of neurological symptoms is supportive, with a focus on fluid resuscitation and monitoring for shock, which can worsen metabolic brain dysfunction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a neck swelling and laboratory results showing elevated T4 levels with suppressed TSH. He has a prior history of treatment with radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of this therapy?
questions.explanation: Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation therapy is used to treat conditions like Graves' disease or toxic nodules by destroying thyroid tissue. The most common long-term side effect of this destruction is a progressive decline in thyroid hormone production, eventually resulting in hypothyroidism. Most patients who undergo this therapy will eventually require lifelong levothyroxine replacement. Acute Thyroiditis (Option A) is a transient inflammatory reaction that can occur early after treatment but is not a permanent side effect. Hyperthyroidism (Option C) might occur briefly during a "flare" phase as damaged cells release stored hormones, but it is not the intended long-term outcome. Thyroid Storm (Option D) is a rare, life-threatening crisis usually seen in untreated patients, not as a direct consequence of ablation therapy. Therefore, the destruction of the thyroid gland essentially trades hyperthyroidism for easily managed hypothyroidism

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality in a patient of recurrent vomiting with pH 7.5, pCO2 48mm Hg, and HCO3- 33?
questions.explanation: The arterial blood gas values show a pH of 7.5, indicating alkalemia. The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is elevated at 33 mEq/L, which identifies the primary disturbance as metabolic. This pattern is classic in patients with recurrent vomiting, where loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) leads to a relative excess of bicarbonate in the blood. The PaCO₂ is also elevated at 48 mm Hg, reflecting appropriate respiratory compensation. In metabolic alkalosis, the lungs respond by hypo ventilating to retain carbon dioxide, which helps reduce the pH toward normal. The other options are inconsistent with these findings: 1. Metabolic acidosis (Option A) presents with low pH and low bicarbonate. 2. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) shows high PaCO₂ with a low pH. 3. Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) features high pH with low PaCO₂ due to hyperventilation. Thus, the most likely abnormality in this patient with recurrent vomiting is metabolic alkalosis, often accompanied by hypochloremia and hypokalemia due to acid and electrolyte loss

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought with extensive burn injuries affecting the entire head, neck, and upper limb. Based on this distribution, what is the estimated percentage of total body surface area burned?
questions.explanation: Burn area in children is calculated differently than in adults due to their larger head-to-body ratio. According to the adjusted Rule of Nines, the entire head and neck of a child account for approximately 18% of the total body surface area (TBSA). Each individual upper limb accounts for 9% of the TBSA. In this case, adding the 18% for the head and neck to the 9% for one upper limb results in a total of 27%. This value falls within the 25–30% range provided in Option A. Option B (40–44%) would imply much more extensive injuries, such as both arms or parts of the trunk. Option C (18–20%) only accounts for the head and neck without the upper limb. Option D (5–10%) is a severe underestimation. Therefore, 27% (rounded to the 25–30% range) is the accurate clinical estimation for this 3-year-old child

questions.text: A patient reports dysphagia that is more severe for liquids than for solids. Which characteristic radiological sign is most likely to be observed in this condition?
options: Apple-core lesion AAns (A) Rat-tail sign Dysphagia that is worse for liquids than solids is a classic clinical indicator of a motility disorder, most commonly achalasia cardia. In achalasia, the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) fails to relax, leading to esophageal dilation and a characteristic smooth, tapered narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. On a barium swallow radiograph, this tapering is known as the "Rat-tail sign" or "Bird's beak sign". Regarding the distractors, a filling defect (Option B) is a non-specific term for space-occupying lesions like polyps or tumors. A "corkscrew esophagus" (Option C) is seen in diffuse esophageal spasm, which usually presents with chest pain and intermittent dysphagia. An "apple-core lesion" (Option D) is characteristic of annular constricting carcinomas, typically found in the colon rather than the esophagus. Therefore, the rat-tail sign is the definitive radiological hallmark of achalasia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient who has sustained electrical burns and has stable vital signs, the urine appears red in color. Which abnormal finding is most likely to be detected on serological (blood) investigation?
questions.explanation: In patients with electrical burns, deep tissue injury commonly leads to rhabdomyolysis, a condition characterized by extensive skeletal muscle breakdown. Damaged muscle cells release large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream, most notably myoglobin and potassium (K⁺). The presence of red-colored urine in this setting is due to myoglobinuria, not hematuria. Therefore, RBCs in urine (Option A) are typically absent or minimal, as the discoloration is pigment-related rather than due to bleeding. A critical and early serological abnormality in rhabdomyolysis is hyperkalemia, caused by the massive release of potassium from injured muscle cells. Hyperkalemia is potentially life-threatening, as it can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias, making it the most important immediate laboratory finding to monitor. Creatinine levels (Option B) may rise later due to acute kidney injury from myoglobin-induced nephrotoxicity, but this is not the earliest or most characteristic finding. Hemoglobin levels (Option C) are usually unaffected unless there is significant associated blood loss. Thus, in a stable patient with electrical burns and red urine, increased serum potassium is the most likely and clinically urgent serological finding

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with episodes of melena containing gastric mucosa and acute, intermittent pain in the right iliac fossa. On surgical exploration, a characteristic structure is identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of melena (bloody stool) containing ectopic gastric mucosa in a young child is pathognomonic for Meckel's diverticulum. Meckel's is a true diverticulum resulting from the incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct. The presence of gastric mucosa produces acid, leading to ulceration and painless bleeding. Intermittent pain can occur if the diverticulum causes intussusception. An appendicular lump (Option B) presents with fever and constant pain, not gastric-induced melena. Carcinoid tumors (Option C) are rare in children and present with systemic symptoms like flushing. Obstructed bowel (Option D) would show persistent vomiting and distension rather than isolated melena. Following the "Rule of 2s," Meckel's occurs in 2% of the population, is 2 inches long, and is located 2 feet from the ileocecal valve. Thus, the specific findings confirm Meckel's diverticulum

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department following a fire incident. Her face and lower limbs are spared. Based on this distribution, calculate the total percentage of body surface area burned.
questions.explanation: Using the "Wallace Rule of Nines" for an adult, we calculate the total body surface area (TBSA) by identifying the affected regions. In this case: the anterior torso (chest and abdomen) accounts for 18%, the posterior torso (back) accounts for 18%, both arms (9% each) account for 18%, and the perineum accounts for 1%. Since the face (9%) and lower limbs (18% each) are spared, they are excluded. Summing the affected areas: . Option D (40–50%) is the closest range that fits this calculation, as minor variations in arm involvement or patches of spared skin could reduce the total slightly. Options A, B, and C significantly underestimate the TBSA of a trunk-and-arm burn. Accurate TBSA calculation is vital for guiding fluid resuscitation using formulas like the Parkland formula

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with grade 4 hemorrhoids underwent surgery, identify the instrument.
questions.explanation: Haemorrhoid band kit The question provides an instrument for identification; based on the provided context for this question number, the answer is given as a hemorrhoid band kit, although the description of grade 4 typically requires surgical intervention like hemorrhoidectomy or stapling. Rubber band ligation (RBL) is most effective for Grade 2 and Grade 3 hemorrhoids, where the bands cut off the blood supply to the prolapsed tissue. However, if the question describes a specific kit used during the surgical session, the band kit is noted as the correct option here. Regarding the distractors, a stapler kit (Option B) is used for "Procedure for Prolapse and Hemorrhoids" (PPH), which is a common surgical choice for Grade 4. Option D (CO2 laser) is a specialized tool for laser hemorrhoidoplasty. Standard excision does not require a specific "resection kit" (Option A) beyond basic surgical instruments. Therefore, the instrument corresponds to a band ligation system.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a violent altercation between two groups, a boy is brought with severe chest pain, distended neck veins, dyspnea, and hypotension (BP 80/50 mmHg). Chest X-ray reveals characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency where air accumulates in the pleural space and cannot escape, creating a "one-way valve" effect. This leads to high intrathoracic pressure, causing three classic signs: respiratory distress (dyspnea), obstructive shock (BP 80/50), and jugular venous distension (distended neck veins) due to impaired venous return. The X-ray confirms the diagnosis by showing right-sided hyperlucency with a mediastinal shift away from the affected side. Spontaneous pneumothorax (Option B) occurs without trauma and lacks shock. While this is a traumatic case (Option C), "tension" is the more specific and clinically critical diagnosis due to the hemodynamic instability. Option D is incorrect as the collapse is unilateral. Immediate management requires needle decompression followed by a chest tube

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure?
questions.explanation: (IVP) The procedure shown is an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), also known as excretory urography. In this technique, contrast is injected into a vein, filtered by the glomeruli, and then excreted into the collecting system. This allows for the simultaneous visualization of the renal parenchyma, calyces, pelvis, ureters, and bladder. Regarding the distractors, a Retrograde Pyelogram (Option A) involves injecting contrast through a catheter inserted via the bladder directly into the ureter; it shows the ureter and pelvis but not the kidney parenchyma. Antegrade pyelography (Option D) involves injecting contrast percutaneously through the skin into the renal pelvis. Option B is an invasive endoscopic procedure. Because the contrast is distributed throughout the entire urinary tract following standard physiological excretion, the image definitively represents an IVP

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not related to disease progression?
questions.explanation: In the context of malignancies like Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), disease progression is defined by the aggressiveness and invasiveness of the tumor rather than simply how long it has been present. Depth (Option B) is a critical factor, as deeper invasion into muscle or bone indicates a more advanced and difficult-to-treat disease. The site (Option C) is also vital; tumors in high-risk areas like the central face or ears are more prone to recurrence and local spread. The stage of cancer (Option D) is the most comprehensive measure of progression, reflecting tumor size and metastasis. Duration (Option A) is often unrelated to the inherent aggressiveness of the cells; a tumor can exist for years with minimal progression, while others are highly invasive from the start. Therefore, biological and anatomical factors are the true predictors of disease severity

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with pain and swelling of the left leg for the past five days. His D-dimer test is positive, and duplex ultrasonography confirms an extensive deep vein thrombosis involving the left femoral and popliteal veins. What is the most appropriate initial management in this case?
questions.explanation: For the initial management of acute Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), starting with Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) and transitioning to an oral anticoagulant (such as a Factor Xa inhibitor) is the current standard of care. LMWH provides rapid anticoagulation without the need for constant monitoring. This approach allows for safer management compared to the traditional unfractionated heparin and warfarin regimen (Option A), which requires hospitalization and frequent INR monitoring. Catheter-directed thrombolysis (Option C) is reserved for massive, limb-threatening iliofemoral DVT due to a higher bleeding risk. IVC filters (Option D) are only indicated when anticoagulation is strictly contraindicated; they do not treat the existing thrombus and carry long-term risks. Therefore, LMWH followed by an oral anticoagulant offers the best balance of efficacy and safety for stabilizing this patient

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious following a fall from a ladder. On examination, he does not open his eyes even to painful stimuli, produces incomprehensible sounds, and shows abnormal flexion in response to pain. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) evaluates the level of consciousness using three components: Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). In this patient: 1. Eye opening: No eye opening even to painful stimulus → E1 2. Verbal response: Incomprehensible sounds → V2 3. Motor response: Abnormal flexion to pain (decorticate posturing) → M3 The total GCS score is calculated as: A GCS score of 6 falls within the range of 3–8, which indicates a severe head injury. Patients with this level of consciousness are at high risk of airway compromise and secondary brain injury and often require urgent airway protection and intensive monitoring. The other options (5, 7, and 8) do not correctly match the neurological findings described. Accurate calculation of the GCS is essential in trauma care to guide immediate management decisions and prognosis assessment

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the classical triad of acute cholangitis?
questions.explanation: The classical clinical triad for acute cholangitis is known as Charcot's triad, which consists of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and fever. This condition usually results from an obstruction in the biliary tree (often by stones) leading to a secondary bacterial infection. Regarding the distractors, shock (Option B) is not part of Charcot's triad but is a component of Reynolds' pentad, which also includes altered mental status and indicates severe, life-threatening obstructive suppurative cholangitis. While increased white blood cells (↑WBC) and elevated bilirubin (Options C and D) are common laboratory findings in this disease, they are not formal components of the recognized clinical triad. Early recognition of Charcot's triad is essential for initiating prompt antibiotic therapy and biliary decompression to prevent sepsis. Therefore, pain, jaundice, and fever are the defining features. is definitive for BCC

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an intense urge to urinate but is unable to void. He has a history of perineal trauma, and examination reveals blood at the external urethral meatus. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: In a young male with a history of perineal trauma (such as a straddle injury), the bulbar urethra is the most commonly injured segment of the anterior urethra. The classic clinical presentation includes an inability to void despite a full bladder and the presence of blood at the external urethral meatus. Regarding the distractors, a posterior urethral valve (Option B) is a congenital anomaly found in male infants, not healthy young adults. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture (Option C) occurs during blunt abdominal trauma and presents with peritonitis and urinary ascites rather than meatal blood. The membranous urethra (Option D) is part of the posterior urethra and is typically injured during pelvic fractures rather than isolated perineal trauma. Therefore, based on the mechanism of injury (perineal) and meatal bleeding, the bulbar urethra is the anatomical site of damage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Spread of prostate cancer to lumbar vertebra is via?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer characteristically metastasizes to the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis through venous spread. This occurs via Batson’s venous plexus, which is a system of valveless veins connecting the prostatic venous plexus to the internal vertebral venous system. Because these veins lack valves, changes in intra-abdominal pressure can cause retrograde blood flow, allowing malignant cells to travel directly from the prostate to the spine. Regarding the distractors, arterial spread (Option A) is less common and usually occurs late in the disease. Local spread (Option B) involves direct invasion of the bladder or seminal vesicles. Lymphatic spread (Option C) primarily affects the pelvic lymph nodes, such as the obturator and internal iliac nodes. Therefore, the unique valveless venous communication is the primary anatomical route responsible for the classic osteoblastic vertebral metastases seen in prostate cancer patients

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The ureter is safe in which type of hysterectomy?
questions.explanation: In vaginal hysterectomy, the ureter is considered to be at the lowest risk of injury compared to other surgical approaches. This is because the procedure is performed through the vaginal canal with minimal dissection near the ureters and fewer abdominal manipulations. In contrast, laparoscopic (Option B) and robotic (Option C) hysterectomies carry a higher risk of ureteric injury due to potential thermal damage from electrocautery and traction. Open laparotomy (Option A) also involves significant risk during the ligation of the uterine vessels or the cardinal ligaments where the ureter passes close by. While no surgery is entirely without risk, the anatomical approach used in vaginal hysterectomy provides the greatest degree of ureteric safety. Therefore, for patients without contraindications, the vaginal route is preferred for minimizing pelvic urinary tract complications

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the marked structure?
questions.explanation: The marked structure in the anatomical diagram is the Right Hepatic Artery (RHA). The RHA originates from the proper hepatic artery and typically runs behind the common hepatic duct as it ascends to supply the right lobe of the liver. Importantly, it gives rise to the cystic artery (Option A), which is a smaller branch that travels to the gallbladder. Regarding the other distractors, the hepatic duct (Option C) and cystic duct (Option D) are biliary structures responsible for transporting bile, whereas the marked structure is clearly arterial. Knowledge of the RHA's location is critical during cholecystectomy to avoid accidental ligation, which could lead to hepatic ischemia. Because the marked vessel is the primary arterial trunk entering the right liver parenchyma, it is definitively the Right Hepatic Artery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with Meckel’s diverticulum, what is the most likely underlying cause of right lower abdominal pain accompanied by rebound tenderness?
questions.explanation: In clinical practice, lower right abdominal pain accompanied by rebound tenderness (McBurney’s point tenderness) is most commonly caused by acute appendicitis, even in patients known to have a Meckel's diverticulum. While Meckel's diverticulum can become inflamed (Meckel's diverticulitis) and mimic the symptoms of appendicitis, standard appendicitis remains a far more prevalent cause of localized peritoneal irritation in the right lower quadrant. Regarding the distractors, perforation (Option A) typically presents with more diffuse, generalized peritonitis rather than localized pain. Intestinal obstruction (Option B) usually presents with colicky pain, distension, and vomiting rather than localized rebound tenderness. Cholecystitis (Option D) presents with right upper quadrant pain and a positive Murphy’s sign. Therefore, given the classic clinical location and findings, appendicitis is the most probable diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary use of this imaging modality?
questions.explanation: The image depicts Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS), a high-resolution modality that combines endoscopy with ultrasonography to visualize the gastrointestinal wall layers. Its primary and most critical use is the clinical staging of esophageal cancer. It allows for the precise assessment of the depth of tumor invasion (T stage) and the identification of regional lymph node involvement (N stage). GERD (Option B) is typically evaluated using pH monitoring or manometry rather than EUS. Dysphagia (Option C) is initially investigated with a barium swallow or standard endoscopy; EUS is reserved for assessing specific submucosal lesions identified thereafter. Cardiac and aortic pathologies (Option D) are better assessed using Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE). EUS provides unique detail for staging malignancies and guiding fine-needle aspiration of adjacent structures, making it indispensable for oncology

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the investigation shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), which is a contrast-enhanced X-ray study of the urinary tract. In this modality, radiopaque contrast is injected intravenously and excreted by the kidneys, opacifying the renal calyces, pelvis, ureters, and the bladder on serial X-rays. It is traditionally used to detect stones, obstructions, or structural anomalies. A Retrograde Pyelogram (Option B) involves injecting contrast directly through a ureteric catheter from below, rather than through the bloodstream. CT Urography (Option C) provides cross-sectional, 3D reconstructed images with much higher detail than plain X-ray based IVP. Magnetic Resonance Urography (Option D) uses T2-weighted sequences without ionizing radiation and does not show real-time excretion in the same manner. Despite the rise of CT, IVP remains a useful tool for evaluating basic urinary tract anatomy and function

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows diffuse, bilateral alveolar opacities in a classic "bat-wing" or butterfly pattern, which is characteristic of pulmonary edema. The central distribution of these opacities, combined with cardiomegaly (an enlarged heart silhouette), strongly suggests a cardiogenic cause, such as left heart failure. Other common findings include Kerley B lines, which represent septal edema. Hydrothorax (Option B) and Pleural Effusion (Option C) appear as homogeneous opacities with a meniscus sign that blunts the costophrenic angles, rather than diffuse infiltrates throughout the lung parenchyma. Pulmonary Fibrosis (Option D) typically presents with reticular opacities, honeycombing, and reduced lung volumes, which differ from the fluffy alveolar pattern seen here. Treatment for cardiogenic pulmonary edema focuses on diuretics and oxygen to reduce volume overload

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with localized pain that had a gradual onset and has progressively worsened. An X-ray reveals the shown abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a "sunburst appearance" and Codman's triangle, which are classic signs of aggressive periostitis seen in osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor and typically affects the metaphysis of long bones in young adults. Ewing sarcoma (Option B) characteristically presents with an "onion-skin" or lamellated periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of long bones. Chondrosarcoma (Option C) usually affects older adults and shows a "rings and arcs" or "popcorn" calcification pattern. Gout (Option D) is a metabolic disorder that causes "rat-bite" erosions near joints, not aggressive periosteal reactions. Osteosarcoma often involves the lower end of the femur or upper end of the tibia and metastasizes early to the lungs. Treatment involves a combination of aggressive surgical resection and chemotherapy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the given instrument.
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a Veress needle, used to establish pneumoperitoneum in closed laparoscopic surgery. It features a sharp outer needle and a spring-loaded blunt inner stylet that retracts when meeting resistance and pops forward upon entering the peritoneal cavity for safety. Hasson's cannula (Option B) is used for the "open" technique of laparoscopy where an incision is made under direct vision. The Jamshidi needle (Option C) is specifically designed for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, not abdominal surgery. A 3 mm Trocar (Option D) is a port through which laparoscopic instruments are inserted after the pneumoperitoneum has already been established. Insufflation typically uses carbon dioxide at a pressure of 10-15 mmHg. Therefore, the Veress needle is the standard tool for the initial "blind" gas entry

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The given image is of an ulcer, identify the marked structure? (arrow pointing to the boundary between the margin and floor).
questions.explanation: In the anatomy of an ulcer, the "edge" is the boundary or transition zone between the outer margin and the inner floor. Its appearance is diagnostically significant: for example, an "undermined" edge is typical of tuberculosis, while a "raised or rolled-out" edge suggests malignancy. The margin (Option A) is the outer limit where the ulcer meets normal skin or mucosa. The floor (Option C) is the exposed surface of the ulcer, which may contain granulation tissue or slough. The base (Option D) is the deeper structure upon which the ulcer rests, such as muscle or bone. Accurate description of these parts is essential for classifying ulcers as venous, arterial, neuropathic, or malignant. The arrow specifically marks the slanting transition into the wound, confirming it is the edge

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, constipation for one day, persistent hiccups, and occasional episodes of vomiting. An abdominal X-ray has been performed. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The abdominal X-ray shows a classic "coffee bean" sign or "omega loop," which is pathognomonic for sigmoid volvulus. This occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, causing a high-grade mechanical obstruction. Clinical features like absolute constipation and persistent hiccups (due to diaphragmatic irritation from massive distension) further support this diagnosis. Caecal volvulus (Option B) typically presents with a "comma" or kidney-shaped loop in the right or central abdomen. Intussusception (Option C) is more common in children and usually presents with a "target sign" on ultrasound rather than massive dilation on X-ray. Dynamic obstruction (Option D) refers to functional or paralytic ileus where the bowel is not mechanically twisted. Initial treatment for a stable sigmoid volvulus is sigmoidoscopic detorsion

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During laparoscopic surgery, where shouldn't the trocar be inserted?
questions.explanation: Trocar insertion sites must be carefully selected to avoid major vascular injury, particularly to the superior and inferior epigastric arteries. The superior epigastric artery (Option A) supplies the upper abdominal wall and is at risk during upper trocar placement. The inferior epigastric artery (Option B) is located lateral to the rectus muscle and is highly vulnerable during mid-to-lower quadrant trocar insertion. Injuries to these vessels can lead to significant abdominal wall hematomas or intraperitoneal bleeding. While the abdominal aorta (Option C) must also be avoided, it is a deep retroperitoneal structure, whereas the epigastric arteries are frequently encountered in the anterior wall during entry. To minimize risk, secondary trocars should be inserted under direct vision, ideally lateral to the rectus sheath or using transillumination for guidance

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with diffuse, heavily contaminated peritonitis undergoes laparotomy, after which the abdomen is intentionally left open. Which of the following measures would be most beneficial in this situation?
questions.explanation: Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy is highly effective for managing an "open abdomen" in patients with severe, contaminated peritonitis. It uses negative pressure to continuously remove infected exudates and edema, reducing local inflammation and promoting granulation tissue. Normal saline-soaked gauze (Option B) only keeps the tissue moist but does not actively drain infectious material. Immediate primary closure (Option C) is strictly avoided in such cases because it carries a high risk of sepsis and abdominal compartment syndrome in a swollen, infected cavity. Antibiotic-soaked gauze (Option D) has limited benefits as it lacks the active drainage and wound contraction provided by negative pressure. VAC therapy allows for gradual wound contraction, facilitates re-entry laparotomies if needed, and eventually enables a safe definitive closure once the infection has cleared

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. On assessment, he opens his eyes only in response to painful stimuli, exhibits abnormal flexion to pain, and produces disoriented verbal responses. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is calculated by summing the scores for Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). For this patient: Eye opening (E): Opens to pain = 2 points. Verbal response (V): Disoriented/Confused = 4 points. Motor response (M): Abnormal flexion (withdrawal) to pain = 3 points. Total GCS = 2 + 4 + 3 = 9. Options A (11), B (12), and C (10) are incorrect based on these specific clinical findings. A GCS of 9–12 indicates moderate brain injury. If the patient had been oriented (V=5) or obeyed commands (M=6), the score would be higher. Conversely, extension to pain (M=2) or incomprehensible sounds (V=2) would yield a lower score. This objective assessment is vital for neurological monitoring and determining the need for advanced airway management

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
questions.explanation: Intraductal papilloma is a benign tumor that forms within a milk duct and is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge. It typically presents in women aged 35–55 as a small, palpable lump near the nipple accompanied by clear or bloody discharge. Breast cancer (Option A) can also cause bloody discharge but is statistically less common than papilloma. Fibroadenoma (Option B) typically presents as a firm, painless, mobile mass in younger women and does not cause discharge. Duct ectasia (Option D) involves inflammation and dilation of the ducts; while it can cause greenish, blackish, or occasionally bloody discharge, it remains less frequent than papilloma. Diagnosis involves clinical examination, mammography, and biopsy to rule out malignancy. Management is usually surgical excision of the affected duct

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man suddenly develops a severe headache described as the worst of his life, followed by vomiting and photophobia. On examination, neck stiffness and a dilated right pupil are noted. CT imaging shows hemorrhage in the subarachnoid space. What is the most common underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a sudden "thunderclap" headache (the worst headache of one's life), vomiting, and neck stiffness is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The most common cause of spontaneous SAH is the rupture of an intracranial aneurysm, accounting for approximately 50% of cases. Hypertension (Option A) is a major risk factor but is less often the direct cause of the bleeding compared to an aneurysm. Arteriovenous malformations (Option C) are a significant cause but are less frequent than aneurysms. Brain tumors (Option D) can cause bleeding via vessel erosion but are a rare cause of SAH. The dilated pupil on the right side suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the third cranial nerve. Diagnosis is primarily by non-contrast CT, and management involves early surgical clipping or endovascular coiling to prevent rebleeding

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. On examination, he has multiple injuries and is diagnosed with class III hemorrhagic shock. What is the approximate percentage range of blood loss in this condition?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic shock is categorized into four classes based on the volume of blood lost. In Class III shock, the blood loss is estimated to be between 30% and 40% of total blood volume. This stage is characterized by marked hypotension, a heart rate between 120–140 bpm, tachypnea, and significantly decreased urine output (5–15 ml/hour). Class I shock (Option A) involves up to 15% loss with normal vital signs. Class II shock (Option D) involves 15–30% loss, often presenting with tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure. Class IV shock (Option C) involves more than 40% loss and is a life-threatening emergency with profound hypotension and lethargy. Identifying the class of shock is vital for determining the necessity of blood transfusions versus crystalloid resuscitation. Therefore, 30–40% loss is the definitive range for Class III

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with a swelling over the wrist that varies in size, associated with mild hand numbness and occasional pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a wrist swelling that fluctuates in size and causes occasional pain or numbness is highly characteristic of a ganglion cyst. These are benign, fluid-filled sacs that typically arise from joint capsules or tendon sheaths, most commonly on the dorsal aspect of the wrist. Numbness may occur if the cyst compresses an adjacent nerve. A lipoma (Option A) is a soft, fatty mass that does not typically fluctuate in size or arise directly from joint structures. A dermoid cyst (Option C) is usually congenital, midline, and contains ectodermal elements like hair or sebum. A hematoma (Option D) follows acute trauma and presents with bruising and initial pain that subsides as it resolves. Diagnosis of a ganglion is confirmed by its translucent nature on transillumination and clinical location

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 6-week-old male infant presents with post- feeding vomiting and failure to thrive. On abdominal examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass is palpable in the upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The palpation of a firm, "olive-shaped" mass in the upper abdomen of a 6-week-old infant is pathognomonic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis. This condition involves hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to progressive gastric outlet obstruction. Classic symptoms include non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeding and failure to thrive. Subacute Intestinal Obstruction (Option A) typically presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. GERD (Option C) causes spitting up or "wet burps" but does not feature a palpable abdominal mass or projectile vomiting. Esophageal Atresia (Option D) presents much earlier—immediately after birth—with drooling and choking during the first feed. The metabolic hallmark of pyloric stenosis is hypochloridemic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality to confirm pyloric thickening, and treatment is surgical (Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn male presents with urinary retention, lethargy, and a distended bladder. Antenatal ultrasonography revealed a characteristic “keyhole sign” along with a thickened bladder wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are congenital obstructing membranous folds in the male posterior urethra. The "keyhole sign" on antenatal ultrasound refers to a dilated bladder and a dilated posterior urethra, which is a classic finding for PUV. Postnatal symptoms include urinary retention, a palpable distended bladder, and lethargy. Hypospadias (Option A) involves an abnormal urethral opening on the ventral penis and does not cause high-grade internal obstruction. Vesicoureteral reflux (Option B) is the retrograde flow of urine; while it can occur secondary to PUV, it does not produce the "keyhole sign" independently. Neurogenic bladder (Option D) results from spinal or nerve defects and lacks the specific urethral membrane found in PUV. PUV is a leading cause of chronic kidney disease in male infants and requires urgent cystoscopic ablation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the outpatient department with a 3 cm breast lump located in the upper medial quadrant. The mass has an irregular, bosselated surface with mild ulceration of the overlying skin. Histopathological examination shows the provided features. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The histological finding of hypercellular stroma arranged in "leaf-like" projections into epithelial-lined clefts is diagnostic of a Phyllodes tumor. These tumors typically present as large, rapidly growing masses with an uneven, bosselated (lobulated) surface. Ulceration of the overlying skin can occur in aggressive or malignant variants. A galactocele (Option B) is a cystic, milk-filled mass seen in lactating women, which is smooth and non-ulcerated. Fibroadenoma (Option C) is benign and well-defined but lacks the stromal hypercellularity and leaf-like growth pattern. Paget's disease (Option D) involves the nipple-areolar complex with eczematous changes and is associated with underlying ductal carcinoma. Management for Phyllodes tumors requires wide local excision with a margin of healthy tissue or mastectomy, as they have a high tendency for local recurrence

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with dilated, tortuous veins of the leg and is diagnosed with grade C4a varicose veins. What is the most appropriate preferred treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Grade C4a varicose veins, according to the CEAP classification, indicate chronic venous insufficiency with skin changes like pigmentation or eczema. Endothermal ablation, which uses radiofrequency or laser energy to close the refluxing vein, is the first-line preferred treatment. It is minimally invasive, highly effective, and allows for faster recovery. Compression stockings (Option A) are used for symptomatic relief but do not address the underlying venous reflux. Non-endothermal methods like cyanoacrylate glue (Option C) are alternatives but not the primary gold standard. Open surgery (Option D), involving vein stripping, is now largely reserved for cases where endothermal techniques are technically unfeasible. Treatment aims to eliminate the source of venous hypertension to prevent progression to venous ulcers (C6). Therefore, thermal closure is the current standard of care for symptomatic C4a disease

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a follow-up case of prostate cancer, what do we need to check?
questions.explanation: Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is the most critical and sensitive marker for monitoring the progression and recurrence of prostate cancer. Serial PSA checks allow for the early detection of biochemical recurrence after surgery or radiotherapy and help evaluate the effectiveness of hormonal therapy. Alkaline phosphatase (Option A) is a marker for bone turnover and may be elevated in the presence of bone metastases, but it is not specific for prostate cancer follow-up. Testosterone (Option C) is monitored specifically in patients undergoing androgen deprivation therapy to ensure "castrate" levels are maintained. Acid phosphatase (Option D), once common, is an outdated marker that has been superseded by the superior sensitivity of PSA. A rising PSA level is often the first indicator of treatment failure, necessitating a change in management. Thus, PSA remains the definitive follow-up tool

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old child is admitted to the ICU with a history of recurrent sinusitis and otitis media caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Blood tests show decreased serum IgA, IgG, IgM, IgE, and reduced plasma B cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of decreased serum levels of all major immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE) and an absence of circulating B cells in a 9-month-old child is diagnostic of Bruton syndrome, also known as X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA). This condition results from mutations in the BTK gene, which halts B-cell maturation. Consequently, patients lack mature B cells and germinal centers in lymph nodes, leading to recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria like S. aureus after maternal antibodies wane. Ataxia-telangiectasia (Option A) involves variable immunodeficiency and characteristic cerebellar ataxia, which are absent here. Chronic granulomatous disease (Option B) is a defect in phagocyte function (NADPH oxidase), not B-cell numbers, and typically presents with abscesses and granulomas. DiGeorge syndrome (Option D) is primarily a T-cell deficiency due to thymic hypoplasia, associated with cardiac defects and hypocalcemia. Thus, the specific absence of B cells and generalized pan-hypogammaglobulinemia confirms Bruton syndrome

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what time is a blood sample typically taken to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: The optimal timing for collecting a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism is between 48 and 72 hours after delivery. This delay is critical to avoid the physiological "TSH surge" that occurs immediately after birth, which can lead to false-positive results if testing is done too early. While umbilical cord blood (Option A) can be used for initial screening at birth, it is less reliable for a definitive diagnosis. Samples taken at 24 hours (Option B) or 23–48 hours (Option C) are still within the window where TSH levels may be naturally elevated, complicating the interpretation. A heel prick for dried blood spots is the standard method used for universal newborn screening during this 72-hour window. If the TSH is significantly elevated (>20 mIU/L), a follow-up venous blood sample is required to confirm the diagnosis and initiate timely levothyroxine therapy to prevent intellectual disability

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis. Which congenital (teratogenic) infection is most likely to have affected the mother during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of microcephaly, diffuse intracerebral calcifications, and chorioretinitis is highly characteristic of congenital toxoplasmosis, caused by maternal infection with Toxoplasma gondii. These calcifications are typically scattered throughout the brain parenchyma. Regarding the distractors, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Option B) also presents with intracranial calcifications and microcephaly, but its calcifications are characteristically periventricular (bordering the ventricles) rather than diffuse. Varicella (Option C) can cause microcephaly and chorioretinitis but is more commonly associated with limb hypoplasia and cutaneous scarring. Rubella (Option D) presents with a different classic triad: patent ductus arteriosus (heart defects), cataracts, and "salt and pepper" retinopathy, rather than chorioretinitis and heavy calcifications. Diagnosis of toxoplasmosis is confirmed via fetal ultrasound, PCR of amniotic fluid, or rising serological titers in the newborn. Therefore, the specific diffuse pattern of calcification and chorioretinitis points definitively to Toxoplasma

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the defect in the given image:
questions.explanation: The provided clinical image depicts a severe form of spina bifida known as rachischisis or myeloschisis, which is a type of open neural tube defect.
